CHAPTER 18 - SOUND AND COMMUNICATION

Introduction

Sound is all around us - the chirping of birds, the ringing of a bell, music from a loudspeaker and the spoken word. Sound is a form of energy that produces the sensation of hearing in our ears. In this chapter we study how sound is produced, how it travels, what kind of wave it is, the quantities that describe it, and how it is used in technology such as SONAR and medical ultrasound. We also look at the structure of the human ear and the basics of communication systems that carry information over long distances.

18.1 PRODUCTION OF SOUND BY VIBRATING BODIES

Sound is always produced by a VIBRATING body. When you strike a tuning fork, pluck a guitar string, beat a drum or speak, some object is set into rapid to-and-fro motion. This vibration disturbs the layers of the surrounding medium (usually air) and the disturbance travels outward as sound. If you touch a ringing bell or a loudspeaker cone you can feel the vibration. When the vibration stops, the sound stops. So the basic rule is: NO VIBRATION, NO SOUND. The to-and-fro motion of the vibrating body pushes the air particles next to it, setting up a chain of pushes and pulls that we hear as sound.

18.2 PROPAGATION OF SOUND - A MATERIAL MEDIUM IS NEEDED

Sound needs a MATERIAL MEDIUM (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through empty space (a vacuum). This can be shown by the bell-in-a-jar experiment: an electric bell is hung inside a glass jar connected to a vacuum pump. As the air is pumped out, the sound of the bell grows fainter and finally cannot be heard at all, even though the hammer is still seen striking the gong. When air is let back in, the sound returns. This proves that sound requires a medium - it is the particles of the medium that carry the disturbance. On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, two astronauts standing side by side cannot hear each other directly; they use radio. Light, by contrast, reaches us from the Sun through the vacuum of space, but the Sun's roaring activity is forever silent to us.

18.3 SOUND AS A LONGITUDINAL WAVE

When a vibrating body moves forward, it pushes the air particles in front of it together, forming a region of HIGH pressure and high density called a COMPRESSION. When it moves back, it leaves behind a region of LOW pressure and low density called a RAREFACTION. As the body vibrates back and forth, a series of compressions and rarefactions travels outward through the air. In such a wave the particles of the medium vibrate BACK AND FORTH along the SAME direction in which the wave travels. A wave in which the particle motion is parallel to the direction of propagation is called a LONGITUDINAL WAVE. Sound is therefore a longitudinal wave. (Compare this with a transverse wave, such as a wave on a rope, where the particles move at right angles to the direction of travel.) It is important to note that the particles of the medium do not travel along with the sound; they only oscillate about their fixed positions and pass the energy along from one layer to the next.

18.4 CHARACTERISTICS OF A SOUND WAVE

A sound wave, like any wave, is described by a few basic quantities:
 - WAVELENGTH (lambda): the distance between two consecutive compressions (or two consecutive rarefactions). It is measured in metres (m).
 - FREQUENCY (f): the number of complete vibrations (or the number of compressions passing a point) per second. Its unit is the hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second.
 - TIME PERIOD (T): the time taken for one complete vibration. T = 1 / f. Its unit is the second (s).
 - AMPLITUDE (A): the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its mean position. It is a measure of how much the pressure rises and falls.
 - SPEED (v): the distance travelled by the sound wave per second, in metres per second (m/s).
These quantities are linked by the WAVE EQUATION:
   v = f x lambda
That is, speed = frequency x wavelength. Since T = 1/f, we can also write v = lambda / T. This single relation lets us find any one quantity if the other two are known.

Worked example 1: A sound wave has frequency 256 Hz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Find its wavelength. Using v = f x lambda, lambda = v / f = 340 / 256 = 1.33 m (approximately).

18.5 PITCH, LOUDNESS AND QUALITY

Three characteristics let us tell one sound from another:
 - PITCH depends on FREQUENCY. A high-frequency sound has a high pitch (shrill, like a whistle or a child's voice); a low-frequency sound has a low pitch (deep, like a drum or a man's voice). Doubling the frequency raises the pitch.
 - LOUDNESS depends on AMPLITUDE. A larger amplitude carries more energy and sounds louder. Hitting a drum harder increases the amplitude and so the loudness, while the pitch stays the same. Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).
 - QUALITY (or TIMBRE) is the characteristic that lets us distinguish two sounds of the same pitch and loudness produced by different sources - for example the same note played on a flute and on a violin. Quality depends on the shape of the waveform (the mixture of frequencies present). It is why we can recognise a friend's voice on the phone.

18.6 SPEED OF SOUND IN DIFFERENT MEDIA AND EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE

The speed of sound depends on the medium. Sound travels FASTEST in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases, because the particles in a solid are packed close together and pass on the disturbance quickly. Approximate speeds at ordinary temperatures are: in steel about 5000 m/s, in water about 1500 m/s, and in air about 340 m/s. In air, the speed of sound INCREASES with temperature - it rises by roughly 0.6 m/s for every 1 degree Celsius rise. This is why sound may travel a little farther on a warm day. The speed of sound in air does NOT depend appreciably on pressure (at constant temperature) and does not depend on the frequency of the sound.

18.7 REFLECTION OF SOUND - ECHO AND REVERBERATION

Like light, sound is REFLECTED when it strikes a hard surface (a wall, a cliff, the floor). The laws of reflection apply: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

ECHO: An echo is the repetition of a sound caused by reflection from a distant surface, heard distinctly after the original sound. To hear a separate echo, the reflected sound must reach the ear at least 0.1 second after the original (this is the persistence of hearing). Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, in 0.1 s sound travels 340 x 0.1 = 34 m. But the sound must travel TO the reflecting surface and BACK, so the minimum distance of the reflector must be 34 / 2 = 17 m. If the reflecting surface is nearer than about 17 m, the echo merges with the original sound and is not heard separately.

Worked example 2 (echo distance): A person claps and hears the echo from a cliff after 3 s. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, how far is the cliff? Total distance travelled by sound = v x t = 340 x 3 = 1020 m. This is the to-and-fro distance, so the distance to the cliff = 1020 / 2 = 510 m.

REVERBERATION: In a large hall, sound is reflected repeatedly from the walls, ceiling and floor. These many overlapping reflections cause the sound to persist even after the source has stopped. This persistence of sound due to repeated reflection is called REVERBERATION. Too much reverberation makes speech unclear, so auditoriums use sound-absorbing materials (curtains, perforated boards, cushioned seats) on the walls and ceiling to reduce it.

18.8 RANGE OF HEARING - AUDIBLE, INFRASONIC AND ULTRASONIC

The human ear can hear sounds only within a certain frequency range, called the AUDIBLE RANGE: from about 20 Hz to 20000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds in this range are AUDIBLE sounds.
 - Sounds of frequency BELOW 20 Hz are called INFRASONIC (or infrasound). They are produced by sources such as earthquakes, large machinery and some animals (elephants, whales). Humans cannot hear them.
 - Sounds of frequency ABOVE 20000 Hz are called ULTRASONIC (or ultrasound). Humans cannot hear them, but animals such as bats, dolphins and dogs can. Bats use ultrasound to navigate and catch prey in the dark.
As people grow older, the upper limit of their audible range usually falls.

18.9 APPLICATIONS OF ULTRASOUND AND SONAR

Because ultrasound has a high frequency and short wavelength, it travels in a well-directed narrow beam and can detect small objects. Its uses include:
 - MEDICAL IMAGING: ultrasound scans are used to form images of internal organs and to monitor the growth of a baby in the womb (a sonogram). It is safe because no harmful radiation is used.
 - CLEANING: ultrasonic vibrations are used to clean delicate parts such as spiral tubes, electronic components and jewellery, dislodging dirt from hard-to-reach places.
 - DETECTING FLAWS: ultrasound is used to detect cracks and flaws inside metal blocks and castings without breaking them.
 - SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging): a device that uses ultrasound to measure the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects such as the seabed, submarines, sunken ships and shoals of fish. A transmitter sends out ultrasonic pulses; these reflect off the object and return to a receiver (detector). By measuring the time t between sending and receiving, and knowing the speed of sound v in water, the depth d is found from:
   2 d = v x t,   so   d = (v x t) / 2
The factor 2 appears because the sound travels down to the object and back.

Worked example 3 (SONAR depth): A SONAR sends a pulse and receives the echo from the seabed after 4 s. If the speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s, find the depth. d = (v x t) / 2 = (1500 x 4) / 2 = 3000 m.

18.10 STRUCTURE AND WORKING OF THE HUMAN EAR

The human ear converts sound waves into nerve signals that the brain interprets. It has three parts:
 - OUTER EAR: the visible part (pinna) collects sound and funnels it through the ear canal to the eardrum (tympanic membrane).
 - MIDDLE EAR: the sound makes the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones (the hammer, anvil and stirrup) amplify these vibrations and pass them to the inner ear.
 - INNER EAR: the vibrations enter a coiled, fluid-filled structure called the COCHLEA. Inside it, sensitive cells convert the vibrations into electrical nerve impulses, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are perceived as sound.

18.11 BASICS OF COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS

Communication is the sending and receiving of information (messages) over a distance. Any communication system has the following basic parts:
 - SIGNAL: the information to be sent (sound, picture, data), converted into an electrical or electromagnetic form.
 - TRANSMITTER: the device that prepares the signal and sends it out (for example a radio station's transmitter, a mobile phone).
 - MEDIUM (or CHANNEL): the path along which the signal travels - wires, optical fibre, or free space for radio waves.
 - RECEIVER: the device that picks up the signal and converts it back into a usable form (a radio set, a television, the other person's phone).
Modern communication uses telephones, radio, television, mobile phones, satellites and the internet to carry information rapidly across the world. Sound itself is a short-range communication; electronic and electromagnetic systems extend it over any distance.

SUMMARY

 - Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and is a form of energy that causes the sensation of hearing.
 - Sound needs a material medium to travel and cannot pass through a vacuum.
 - Sound is a longitudinal wave consisting of compressions and rarefactions.
 - A sound wave is described by wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude and speed, related by v = f x lambda (and T = 1/f).
 - Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude, and quality (timbre) on the waveform.
 - Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases; in air its speed increases with temperature.
 - Reflection of sound gives echoes (minimum reflector distance about 17 m) and reverberation (repeated reflections in a hall).
 - The audible range is 20 Hz to 20000 Hz; below is infrasonic, above is ultrasonic.
 - Ultrasound is used in medical imaging, cleaning, flaw detection and SONAR; SONAR depth is found from d = (v x t) / 2.
 - The human ear (outer, middle, inner) converts sound into nerve signals; a communication system has a signal, transmitter, medium and receiver.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Sound and Communication (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science and Technology (212) official Worksheet-18 for Lesson 18. Attempt all questions. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s and in water as 1500 m/s unless stated otherwise.

questions.question: How is sound produced? Give two everyday examples and state what happens to the sound when the source stops vibrating.
questions.answer: Sound is produced by a VIBRATING body. The rapid to-and-fro motion of the body disturbs the layers of the surrounding medium, and this disturbance travels outward as sound. Examples: (1) a plucked guitar string vibrates and produces a note; (2) a struck tuning fork or a beaten drum vibrates and produces sound. When the source stops vibrating, the sound stops - no vibration means no sound. You can verify this by touching a ringing bell: while it sounds it vibrates, and damping the vibration silences it.
questions.explanation: Sound requires a vibrating source; stopping the vibration stops the sound.

questions.question: Describe the bell-in-a-jar experiment and state what it proves about the propagation of sound.
questions.answer: An electric bell is suspended inside a glass jar that is connected to a vacuum pump. When the bell is switched on with air in the jar, its ringing is clearly heard. As the air is gradually pumped out, the sound grows fainter and finally cannot be heard at all, even though the hammer is still seen striking the gong. When air is allowed back into the jar, the sound returns. This proves that sound needs a MATERIAL MEDIUM to travel and cannot pass through a vacuum, because it is the particles of the medium that carry the disturbance.
questions.explanation: Sound fades as the medium is removed - sound cannot travel through vacuum.

questions.question: Explain why sound is called a longitudinal wave. How does it differ from a transverse wave?
questions.answer: In a sound wave the particles of the medium vibrate BACK AND FORTH along the SAME direction in which the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions. Because the particle motion is parallel to the direction of propagation, sound is a LONGITUDINAL wave. In a TRANSVERSE wave (for example a wave on a rope or a water-surface ripple) the particles move at RIGHT ANGLES to the direction in which the wave travels, forming crests and troughs. So the key difference is the direction of particle vibration relative to the direction of wave travel: parallel for longitudinal, perpendicular for transverse.
questions.explanation: Longitudinal: particle motion parallel to propagation. Transverse: perpendicular.

questions.question: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels with a speed of 340 m/s in air. Calculate its wavelength and its time period.
questions.answer:
Given f = 500 Hz, v = 340 m/s.
Wavelength: from v = f x lambda, lambda = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m.
Time period: T = 1 / f = 1 / 500 = 0.002 s = 2 x 10^-3 s.
So the wavelength is 0.68 m and the time period is 0.002 s.

questions.question: Distinguish between the pitch and the loudness of a sound. On what physical quantity does each depend?
questions.answer: PITCH is how high or low a sound seems. It depends on the FREQUENCY of the sound wave: a high frequency gives a high (shrill) pitch, such as a whistle, while a low frequency gives a low (deep) pitch, such as a drum. LOUDNESS is how strong or faint a sound seems. It depends on the AMPLITUDE of the sound wave: a larger amplitude carries more energy and sounds louder. For example, striking a drum harder increases the amplitude and so the loudness, but the pitch stays the same. So pitch depends on frequency and loudness depends on amplitude.

questions.question: Differentiate between an echo and reverberation.
questions.answer: An ECHO is the distinct repetition of a sound heard after it is reflected from a single distant surface (such as a cliff or a wall). To hear it as separate from the original sound, the reflected sound must arrive at least 0.1 s later, which means the reflecting surface must be at least about 17 m away. REVERBERATION is the persistence of sound caused by MANY repeated reflections from the walls, ceiling and floor of a closed space such as a hall. The overlapping reflections blend together so that the sound continues even after the source has stopped, rather than being heard as a clear separate repetition. Auditoriums use sound-absorbing materials to reduce excessive reverberation.
questions.explanation: Echo: single distinct reflection (>=17 m). Reverberation: many overlapping reflections in a hall.

questions.question: A person stands in front of a cliff, claps once, and hears the echo after 2 s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, find the distance of the cliff from the person.
questions.answer:
The sound travels to the cliff and back in the time of the echo.
Total distance travelled = speed x time = 340 x 2 = 680 m.
This is the to-and-fro (down-and-back) distance, so the distance to the cliff = 680 / 2 = 340 m.
The cliff is 340 m away.
questions.explanation: Distance to reflector = (v x t) / 2 because sound travels both ways.

questions.question: State the audible range of frequencies for humans. Define infrasonic and ultrasonic sounds and give one source of each.
questions.answer: The AUDIBLE RANGE for a normal human ear is about 20 Hz to 20000 Hz (20 kHz). INFRASONIC sounds have frequency BELOW 20 Hz and cannot be heard by humans; a source is an earthquake (also large machinery and elephants). ULTRASONIC sounds have frequency ABOVE 20000 Hz and also cannot be heard by humans; a source is a bat (also dolphins and ultrasonic whistles). The upper limit of hearing usually decreases as a person grows older.
questions.explanation: Audible 20 Hz-20000 Hz; infrasonic below, ultrasonic above.

questions.question: A SONAR device on a ship sends an ultrasonic pulse towards the seabed and receives its echo after 5 s. If the speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s, calculate the depth of the sea.
questions.answer:
In SONAR the sound travels down to the seabed and back in the recorded time.
Using 2 d = v x t, the depth d = (v x t) / 2.
d = (1500 x 5) / 2 = 7500 / 2 = 3750 m.
The depth of the sea is 3750 m. (The factor 2 is used because the pulse travels both down and back up.)

questions.question: Describe the structure and working of the human ear, naming its three main parts. Then list the four basic parts of a communication system.
questions.answer:
The human ear converts sound waves into nerve signals and has three parts.
1. OUTER EAR: the visible pinna collects sound and directs it through the ear canal to the eardrum (tympanic membrane).
2. MIDDLE EAR: the sound makes the eardrum vibrate. Three small bones - the hammer, anvil and stirrup - amplify the vibrations and pass them on to the inner ear.
3. INNER EAR: the vibrations enter the COCHLEA, a coiled fluid-filled structure. Sensitive cells in the cochlea convert the vibrations into electrical nerve impulses, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are perceived as sound.

The four basic parts of a communication system are: (a) SIGNAL - the information to be sent, in electrical/electromagnetic form; (b) TRANSMITTER - the device that prepares and sends the signal; (c) MEDIUM (channel) - the path along which the signal travels (wire, optical fibre or free space); (d) RECEIVER - the device that picks up the signal and converts it back into a usable form.
questions.explanation: Outer (pinna, canal, eardrum), middle (three bones), inner (cochlea, auditory nerve); communication = signal, transmitter, medium, receiver.

questions.explanation: An echo is reflected sound from a distant surface.

questions.explanation: A compression is a region of high pressure.

questions.explanation: Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude.

questions.question: Sound travels faster in steel than in air.

questions.question: Bats can hear ultrasonic sounds.

questions.question: Sound is produced by a ____ body.
Sound cannot travel through a ____.
Sound travels as a ____ wave.
A region of high pressure in a sound wave is called a ____.
A region of low pressure in a sound wave is called a ____.
The unit of frequency is the ____.
For a wave, v = f x ____.
The time period is the ____ of the frequency.
The pitch of a sound depends on its ____.
The loudness of a sound depends on its ____.
In air, the speed of sound ____ as the temperature rises.
The persistence of sound due to repeated reflections in a hall is called ____.
The audible range of frequency for humans is 20 Hz to ____ Hz.
Sound of frequency above 20000 Hz is called ____ sound.
In a communication system, the device that sends the signal is the ____.
questions.explanation: It prepares and sends the signal.

questions.question: State two conditions necessary for the production and hearing of sound.
questions.answer: Two conditions are: (1) there must be a VIBRATING body to produce the sound; and (2) there must be a MATERIAL MEDIUM (solid, liquid or gas) between the source and the listener to carry the sound, since sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.question: Why is there no sound on the surface of the Moon?
questions.answer: The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no material medium (no air) to carry sound. Since sound needs particles of a medium to travel and cannot pass through a vacuum, sounds produced on the Moon cannot reach a listener directly. Astronauts therefore communicate by radio waves, which are electromagnetic and need no medium.
questions.explanation: No atmosphere = no medium = no sound.

questions.question: What is meant by compression and rarefaction in a sound wave?
questions.answer: A COMPRESSION is a region of a sound wave where the particles of the medium are pushed close together, giving high pressure and high density. A RAREFACTION is a region where the particles are spread apart, giving low pressure and low density. As the source vibrates, alternate compressions and rarefactions travel outward through the medium.
questions.explanation: Compression: high pressure; rarefaction: low pressure.

questions.question: Do the particles of the medium move along with a sound wave? Explain.
questions.answer: No. The particles of the medium only OSCILLATE back and forth about their fixed mean positions; they do not travel along with the wave. Each particle passes the disturbance (energy) on to the next layer and then returns. So the wave (energy) moves forward, but the medium as a whole stays in place. This is why a sound can travel across a room while the air does not flow across with it.
questions.explanation: Only energy travels; particles oscillate in place.

questions.question: A sound wave has a wavelength of 0.5 m and a frequency of 680 Hz. Calculate its speed.
questions.answer:
Using the wave relation v = f x lambda:
v = 680 x 0.5 = 340 m/s.
The speed of the sound wave is 340 m/s.
questions.explanation: v = f x lambda = 680 x 0.5 = 340 m/s.

questions.question: A source produces 1200 waves in 4 seconds. If the wavelength is 1.1 m, find the frequency and the speed of the wave.
questions.answer:
Frequency f = number of waves / time = 1200 / 4 = 300 Hz.
Speed v = f x lambda = 300 x 1.1 = 330 m/s.
So the frequency is 300 Hz and the speed is 330 m/s.
questions.explanation: f = 1200/4 = 300 Hz; v = f x lambda = 330 m/s.

questions.question: Define wavelength and frequency of a sound wave and give their SI units.
questions.answer: WAVELENGTH (lambda) is the distance between two consecutive compressions (or two consecutive rarefactions) of a sound wave; its SI unit is the metre (m). FREQUENCY (f) is the number of complete vibrations made per second; its SI unit is the hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second.
questions.explanation: Wavelength in metres; frequency in hertz.

questions.question: What is meant by the quality (timbre) of a sound? Give an example.
questions.answer: QUALITY or TIMBRE is the characteristic of a sound that lets us distinguish two sounds of the SAME pitch and SAME loudness produced by DIFFERENT sources. It depends on the shape of the waveform (the mixture of frequencies present). For example, the same note played on a flute and on a violin sounds different because of their different quality; this is also how we recognise different people's voices.
questions.explanation: Timbre distinguishes sources; depends on waveform.

questions.question: Two sounds have the same loudness, but one is much shriller than the other. Which physical quantity differs, and how?
questions.answer: The two sounds differ in FREQUENCY, not amplitude. 'Shriller' means a higher PITCH, and pitch depends on frequency: the shriller sound has a HIGHER frequency. Since both sounds have the same loudness, their amplitudes are the same. So the difference in shrillness is entirely due to a difference in frequency.
questions.explanation: Same loudness = same amplitude; shriller = higher frequency.

questions.question: Arrange solids, liquids and gases in order of the speed of sound through them, and explain why.
questions.answer: The speed of sound is greatest in SOLIDS, less in LIQUIDS, and least in GASES (solids > liquids > gases). This is because the particles in a solid are packed very close together, so a disturbance is passed from one particle to the next very quickly. In liquids the particles are farther apart, and in gases they are much farther apart, so the disturbance is passed on more slowly. Approximate values: steel about 5000 m/s, water about 1500 m/s, air about 340 m/s.
questions.explanation: Closer particles pass on the disturbance faster: solids fastest.

questions.question: A boy shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 1.5 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff? If he moves 85 m closer, what will the new echo time be?
questions.answer:
First distance: total path = v x t = 340 x 1.5 = 510 m. This is the to-and-fro distance, so distance to the cliff = 510 / 2 = 255 m.
After moving 85 m closer, new distance = 255 - 85 = 170 m. The to-and-fro path is now 2 x 170 = 340 m, so the new echo time = distance / speed = 340 / 340 = 1.0 s.
The cliff is 255 m away, and the new echo time is 1.0 s.

questions.question: Why must a reflecting surface be at least about 17 m away to produce a distinct echo?
questions.answer: To hear an echo as SEPARATE from the original sound, the reflected sound must reach the ear at least 0.1 s after the original (this is the persistence of hearing). In 0.1 s, sound travels v x t = 340 x 0.1 = 34 m. But the sound must go to the reflecting surface and come back, so this 34 m is the to-and-fro path. The distance to the surface must therefore be at least 34 / 2 = 17 m. If the surface is nearer, the echo merges with the original sound and cannot be heard separately.

questions.question: How is excessive reverberation in a large hall reduced?
questions.answer: Reverberation is the persistence of sound due to repeated reflections from the walls, ceiling and floor. Excessive reverberation makes speech unclear. It is reduced by covering the walls and ceiling with SOUND-ABSORBING materials such as heavy curtains, carpets, perforated boards and cushioned (upholstered) seats. These materials absorb sound energy instead of reflecting it, so the repeated reflections die away quickly and speech and music sound clear.
questions.explanation: Use sound-absorbing materials to cut repeated reflections.

questions.question: List three applications of ultrasound.
questions.answer: Three applications of ultrasound are: (1) MEDICAL IMAGING - forming images of internal organs and monitoring a baby in the womb (sonography); (2) CLEANING - ultrasonic cleaning of delicate parts such as spiral tubes, electronic components and jewellery; (3) SONAR - measuring the depth of the sea and detecting underwater objects such as submarines and shoals of fish. (Detecting cracks/flaws in metal castings is another use.)

questions.question: A SONAR sends a signal and the echo returns from the seabed after 3 s. If the speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s, find the depth of the sea.
questions.answer:
Using 2d = v x t, so depth d = (v x t) / 2.
d = (1500 x 3) / 2 = 4500 / 2 = 2250 m.
The depth of the sea is 2250 m. The factor 2 is used because the signal travels down to the seabed and back up.

questions.question: Explain how SONAR is used to find the depth of the sea.
questions.answer: SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) has a transmitter that sends short ultrasonic pulses downward into the sea and a receiver (detector) that picks up the echo reflected from the seabed. The time t between sending the pulse and receiving the echo is measured. Knowing the speed of sound v in sea water, the depth d is found from 2d = v x t, i.e. d = (v x t)/2. The factor 2 appears because the sound travels down to the seabed and back to the ship.
questions.explanation: Send pulse, time the echo, d = (v x t)/2.

questions.question: Name the three main parts of the human ear and state the function of each.
questions.answer: (1) OUTER EAR: the pinna collects sound and the ear canal carries it to the eardrum. (2) MIDDLE EAR: the eardrum vibrates and three small bones (hammer, anvil, stirrup) amplify the vibrations and pass them inward. (3) INNER EAR: the cochlea converts the vibrations into nerve impulses that travel along the auditory nerve to the brain.
questions.explanation: Outer collects, middle amplifies, inner converts to nerve signals.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe the four basic parts of a communication system.
questions.answer: (1) SIGNAL - the information (sound, picture or data) to be sent, put into electrical or electromagnetic form. (2) TRANSMITTER - the device that prepares the signal and sends it out. (3) MEDIUM (channel) - the path the signal travels along, such as a wire, optical fibre or free space. (4) RECEIVER - the device that picks up the signal and converts it back into a usable form (sound, picture or data).

questions.question: How is the working of the human ear similar to a communication system?
questions.answer: In both, information is captured, carried and converted. In the ear, the SIGNAL is the sound wave; the outer and middle ear act like a TRANSMITTER/collector that gathers and amplifies it; the vibrations are carried inward (the MEDIUM); and the cochlea with the auditory nerve acts like a RECEIVER, converting the vibrations into nerve impulses that the brain interprets. Likewise a communication system has a signal, a transmitter, a medium and a receiver - so the ear is a natural example of receiving and converting a signal.
questions.explanation: Both capture a signal, carry it, and convert it for interpretation.

questions.question: The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. What is the wavelength of a sound of frequency 850 Hz?
questions.answer:
Using v = f x lambda, the wavelength lambda = v / f = 340 / 850 = 0.4 m.
The wavelength is 0.4 m.

questions.question: State the laws of reflection of sound.
questions.answer: Sound obeys the same laws of reflection as light: (1) the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection; and (2) the incident sound, the reflected sound and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. These laws explain echoes and the working of devices such as megaphones and sound boards.
questions.explanation: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection; all in one plane.

questions.question: Give one piece of evidence that sound needs a medium to travel.
questions.answer: The bell-in-a-jar experiment is the evidence: when an electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar and the air is pumped out, the sound becomes fainter and finally stops, even though the hammer is still seen striking. When air is let back in, the sound returns. This shows sound cannot travel without a material medium.
questions.explanation: Bell-in-a-jar: sound fades as the medium is removed.

questions.question: A drummer hits a drum harder and then strikes a smaller, tighter drum. Explain the change in loudness and the change in pitch.
questions.answer: Hitting the same drum HARDER increases the AMPLITUDE of the vibration, so the sound becomes LOUDER, while its pitch stays the same. Striking a smaller, tighter drum increases the FREQUENCY of vibration, so the sound has a HIGHER PITCH (it sounds higher). So loudness is controlled by how hard it is struck (amplitude) and pitch is controlled by the size/tightness of the drum (frequency).
questions.explanation: Harder = more amplitude = louder; tighter/smaller = higher frequency = higher pitch.

questions.question: A man standing between two parallel cliffs claps once and hears two echoes. Explain why, and state which echo he hears first.
questions.answer: The clap travels in both directions and is reflected by EACH cliff, so two separate echoes return. The man hears the echo from the NEARER cliff first, because the sound to it and back covers a shorter path and so returns in a shorter time. The echo from the farther cliff arrives later. If the cliffs are far enough apart, the two echoes are heard distinctly; the time gap depends on the difference in the two distances.
questions.explanation: Two reflectors give two echoes; the nearer cliff's echo arrives first.

questions.question: A ship's SONAR finds the seabed at a depth of 1800 m. If the speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s, how long after sending the pulse will the echo be received?
questions.answer:
The echo time is found from 2d = v x t, so t = 2d / v.
t = (2 x 1800) / 1500 = 3600 / 1500 = 2.4 s.
The echo will be received 2.4 s after the pulse is sent.

questions.question: Why is sound classified as a mechanical wave?
questions.answer: Sound is called a MECHANICAL wave because it needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel and cannot pass through a vacuum. It propagates by the to-and-fro motion of the particles of the medium, which pass the disturbance from one layer to the next. Waves that require a medium in this way are mechanical waves, in contrast to electromagnetic waves (like light), which can travel through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Needs a medium and uses particle motion - hence mechanical.

questions.question: If a wave has a time period of 0.005 s, what is its frequency?
questions.answer:
Frequency is the reciprocal of the time period: f = 1 / T = 1 / 0.005 = 200 Hz.
The frequency is 200 Hz.

questions.question: The speed of sound in air at 0 degrees C is about 331 m/s and it increases by about 0.6 m/s per degree C. Estimate the speed at 25 degrees C.
questions.answer:
Increase in speed = 0.6 x 25 = 15 m/s.
Speed at 25 degrees C = 331 + 15 = 346 m/s (about).
So the speed of sound is approximately 346 m/s at 25 degrees C.

questions.question: What is the role of the eardrum and the three small bones in hearing?
questions.answer: The EARDRUM (tympanic membrane) is a thin membrane that VIBRATES when sound waves from the ear canal strike it. The three small bones of the middle ear - the hammer, anvil and stirrup - then AMPLIFY these vibrations and transmit them to the inner ear (the cochlea). Together they convert the incoming sound into stronger mechanical vibrations suitable for the inner ear to process.
questions.explanation: Eardrum vibrates; the three bones amplify and pass on the vibrations.

questions.question: On what does the loudness of a sound depend, and in what unit is it measured?
questions.answer: The loudness of a sound depends on the AMPLITUDE of the sound wave - a larger amplitude carries more energy and is heard as a louder sound. Loudness (more precisely, the sound level) is measured in DECIBELS (dB).
questions.explanation: Loudness depends on amplitude; measured in decibels.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A physics teacher demonstrates a tuning fork that vibrates 480 times each second. The class records that the sound travels through the air of the room at 336 m/s. (a) State the frequency of the tuning fork. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the sound it produces. (c) Find the time period of one vibration. (d) If a second fork of 960 Hz is used in the same air, how does its wavelength compare with the first?
questions.answer:
(a) The frequency equals the number of vibrations per second = 480 Hz.
(b) Using v = f x lambda, lambda = v / f = 336 / 480 = 0.7 m.
(c) Time period T = 1 / f = 1 / 480 = 0.00208 s (about 2.08 x 10^-3 s).
(d) For the 960 Hz fork, lambda = 336 / 960 = 0.35 m. Since the frequency is doubled (480 to 960) at the same speed, the wavelength is HALVED (0.7 m to 0.35 m).
questions.explanation: Apply v = f x lambda and T = 1/f; doubling f halves lambda at fixed v.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A girl standing in an open field claps her hands once near a tall building. She hears a clear echo 0.8 s later. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m/s. (a) What is an echo? (b) Calculate the distance of the building from the girl. (c) If she now stands only 10 m from a wall, will she hear a distinct echo? Why or why not? (d) Name the effect heard when a sound is repeatedly reflected inside a closed hall.
questions.answer:
(a) An echo is the distinct repetition of a sound heard after it is reflected from a distant surface.
(b) Total path = v x t = 340 x 0.8 = 272 m. This is the to-and-fro distance, so distance to the building = 272 / 2 = 136 m.
(c) No. A distinct echo needs the reflector to be at least about 17 m away (so the reflected sound returns at least 0.1 s later). At 10 m the reflected sound returns in less than 0.1 s, so it merges with the original sound and no separate echo is heard.
(d) Reverberation.
questions.explanation: Echo distance = (v x t)/2; minimum 17 m; repeated reflections in a hall = reverberation.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A research ship uses SONAR to map the ocean floor. It sends an ultrasonic pulse straight down and receives the reflected echo after 4 s. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. (a) What does SONAR stand for? (b) Why is ultrasound, rather than audible sound, used in SONAR? (c) Calculate the depth of the sea at this point. (d) Why is the factor of 2 used in the calculation?
questions.answer:
(a) SONAR stands for Sound Navigation And Ranging.
(b) Ultrasound has a high frequency and short wavelength, so it travels in a well-directed narrow beam and can detect small or distant objects clearly; it is also inaudible and not affected by ordinary noise.
(c) Using 2d = v x t, depth d = (v x t)/2 = (1500 x 4)/2 = 6000/2 = 3000 m.
(d) The factor of 2 is used because the pulse travels down to the seabed AND back up to the ship - twice the depth.
questions.explanation: SONAR uses ultrasound; d = (v x t)/2 = 3000 m; factor 2 for the down-and-back path.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. When a friend speaks to you across a room, the sound enters your ear and you understand the message; this is similar to how a radio receives a broadcast. (a) Name the three main parts of the human ear. (b) Which part converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses? (c) Name the four basic parts of a communication system. (d) In the radio example, which part of the communication system does your ear correspond to?
questions.answer:
(a) The three main parts are the outer ear, the middle ear and the inner ear.
(b) The cochlea (in the inner ear) converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain.
(c) The four basic parts are the signal, the transmitter, the medium (channel) and the receiver.
(d) Your ear corresponds to the RECEIVER, because it picks up the incoming signal (sound) and converts it into a form (nerve impulses) that the brain can interpret.
questions.explanation: Ear: outer/middle/inner; cochlea converts to nerve impulses; comm system = signal/transmitter/medium/receiver; ear = receiver.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A student rings an electric bell inside a sealed glass jar connected to a vacuum pump. As the pump removes the air, the bell's sound becomes fainter and finally cannot be heard, although the hammer is still seen striking the gong. Air is then let back in. (a) What happens to the sound when air is let back in? (b) What property of sound does this experiment demonstrate? (c) Why does the sound fade as air is removed? (d) Would this experiment work the same way with light from a lamp inside the jar?
questions.answer:
(a) When air is let back in, the bell's sound is heard clearly again.
(b) It demonstrates that sound needs a material medium to travel and cannot pass through a vacuum.
(c) The sound fades because there are fewer and fewer air particles to carry the disturbance; with the air removed there is no medium to carry the sound.
(d) No. Light is an electromagnetic wave and does not need a medium, so a lamp inside the jar would still be seen even in a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Bell-in-a-jar shows sound needs a medium; light differs as it needs none.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A long, soft spring (slinky) is pushed and pulled along its length at one end. A pattern of close-together and spread-out coils moves along the spring, just like the layers of air in a sound wave. (a) What type of wave does this model? (b) What do the close-together coils represent? (c) What do the spread-out coils represent? (d) In which direction do the coils of the spring move compared with the direction of the wave?
questions.answer:
(a) It models a longitudinal wave, the same kind as a sound wave.
(b) The close-together coils represent compressions (regions of high pressure and density).
(c) The spread-out coils represent rarefactions (regions of low pressure and density).
(d) The coils move back and forth ALONG the same direction in which the wave travels (parallel to the wave), which is the defining feature of a longitudinal wave.
questions.explanation: Slinky models a longitudinal wave: compressions, rarefactions, parallel particle motion.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. In a music class, a student plays the same note 'A' first softly and then loudly on a guitar, and then plays the same note on a flute. (a) When the note is played louder, which property of the sound wave increases? (b) Does the pitch change between the soft and loud guitar notes? (c) The flute and guitar play the same note at the same loudness, yet they sound different. Which property accounts for this? (d) On what does that property depend?
questions.answer:
(a) Playing louder increases the amplitude of the sound wave.
(b) No. The pitch stays the same because pitch depends on frequency, and the frequency of the note 'A' is unchanged; only the loudness (amplitude) changes.
(c) The difference is due to the quality (timbre) of the sound.
(d) Quality (timbre) depends on the shape of the waveform - the particular mixture of frequencies produced by each instrument.
questions.explanation: Loud = more amplitude; same pitch = same frequency; flute vs guitar differ in timbre (waveform).

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A man fires a gun and starts a stopwatch at the same instant. He hears the echo from a distant hill 3 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. (a) Write the relation used to find the distance of a reflector from the echo time. (b) Calculate the distance of the hill. (c) Sound travels faster in steel than in air. State whether the same gun's sound would reach a listener through a long steel rail sooner or later than through air. (d) Give the approximate speed of sound in air and in steel.
questions.answer:
(a) Distance of reflector d = (v x t)/2, where v is the speed of sound and t is the echo time (the factor 2 is for the to-and-fro path).
(b) d = (340 x 3)/2 = 1020/2 = 510 m. The hill is 510 m away.
(c) Sooner. Because sound travels much faster in steel than in air, the sound would reach the listener through the steel rail sooner than through the air.
(d) Speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s and in steel about 5000 m/s.
questions.explanation: Echo distance d = (v x t)/2 = 510 m; sound is faster in steel than air.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A doctor uses an ultrasound machine to look at a patient's internal organs, while across town an engineer uses ultrasonic waves to clean fine machine parts. (a) What is the frequency range of ultrasonic sound? (b) Can humans hear ultrasound? (c) Why is ultrasound suitable for imaging internal organs? (d) Why is ultrasound effective for cleaning fine or hard-to-reach parts?
questions.answer:
(a) Ultrasonic sound has a frequency above 20000 Hz (20 kHz).
(b) No, humans cannot hear ultrasound, as it lies above the audible range.
(c) Ultrasound has a short wavelength and travels in a well-directed narrow beam, so it can form clear images of internal organs; it is also safe because it uses no harmful radiation.
(d) Its rapid, high-frequency vibrations dislodge dirt and particles from fine grooves and hard-to-reach places, cleaning parts without damaging them.
questions.explanation: Ultrasound > 20000 Hz, inaudible; narrow beam for imaging; vibrations dislodge dirt for cleaning.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A new school auditorium has bare concrete walls and a high ceiling. During the first assembly, the principal's speech sounds blurred and words seem to run into each other. (a) Name the effect that is blurring the speech. (b) What causes this effect in the hall? (c) Suggest two ways to reduce it. (d) Explain how these measures help.
questions.answer:
(a) The effect is reverberation.
(b) It is caused by the sound being reflected repeatedly from the hard walls, ceiling and floor; these overlapping reflections persist and blur the speech.
(c) Two ways: (i) cover the walls and ceiling with sound-absorbing materials such as curtains, carpets or perforated boards; (ii) use cushioned (upholstered) seats and possibly a false ceiling.
(d) These soft, porous materials ABSORB sound energy instead of reflecting it, so the repeated reflections die away quickly and the speech becomes clear.
questions.explanation: Reverberation from hard surfaces; reduce with sound-absorbing materials that absorb rather than reflect.
